turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit. Obs are done, I'll leave them with you. Blood pressure one hundred and forty-six over ninety-two, pulse eighty-four. Doctor's running late, the computers are on a go-slow.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Brilliant. My head's pounding and I've been sitting out there since eight.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, sorry, Kyle Maseko, I'm Dr Pillay. This screen has frozen on me again, give me a second. Right. What can I do for you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Headaches. I already told the lady at the desk.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Headaches. I've had them for years, but it's different now. Worse when I wake up. I'm sick of it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Worse on waking. How long have the headaches been going, overall?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Five-ish years. Maybe longer. I don't keep a diary.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He always says migraines. His mom was the same, her whole life, proper migraines.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Migraines. We don't need the family history lecture.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the morning ones, when did that change start?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Round about.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's a month, Kyle. Since my brother's wedding, and that weekend was a month back. You left the braai early, remember, you were pale.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The braai doesn't matter, and it has not been a month.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. You don't agree, so I'll put somewhere between two weeks and a month and move on. Any vomiting with these?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't vomit. It's just the headache.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Where do you feel it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Both sides, some days more the left. Throbbing. Like a pulse behind the eye, but both eyes, sort of.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And this morning, out of ten?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Seven. Eight when I first sit up. Can we not do the numbers thing, hey.
[SEG0021] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, he's also snoring like a tractor, every night. And he's exhausted. Nods off on the couch before seven. I keep telling him.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not snoring. She's exaggerating. And I'm not tired, I'm irritated, there's a difference. Can we stick to the headache.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): One second, a popup. What medicines are you on for this?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, three times a day, sometimes four if the workshop's loud. And sumatriptan when it really kicks off.
[SEG0025] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, quick one. The repeat on his file says sumatriptan one hundred milligrams, when required. I'm reading it off so you don't have to dig.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That file is old. I take fifty. The hundred made my chest go tight, so the chemist changed it. I've said this.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fifty or a hundred? Repeat it, because I'm staring at one hundred milligrams.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams. I don't care what the computer thinks.
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Whichever it is, he's taking them two or three times a week. More if it's a bad week.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Two or three times a week. And the Panado most days?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, most days, otherwise I can't work. I'm a panel beater, the noise sets the pain off. I can't exactly work in silence.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noise makes it worse. What helps?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Dark room, lying down, quiet. Panado takes the edge off. Not always.

[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Oh, side thing, my sister lives on biotin gummies, reckons they fix energy. I got him a bottle, he never took a single one. And I didn't touch my dad's metformin, that's my dad, he's the diabetic, not Kyle.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, Nadine, please. Not your dad's tablets. Not today.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't go there. Any double vision? Weakness in the arms or legs?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. Eyes are fine. I just want this sorted, something stronger maybe.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the neck stiff?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come forward a bit. Pupils are equal and reacting to light, no droop of the face. Grip is strong both sides and finger-nose is fine. No stiffness in the neck, that's the quick version.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): See. Normal. So a script and I can go, ja?
[SEG0042] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Tell him about the bathroom, Kyle. Don't give me that look.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, alright, I threw up twice this morning, the coffee first and then just bile. Yesterday morning as well, once. I didn't want a scene in the waiting room.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again. You vomited?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, once yesterday and twice today. I said I don't vomit because usually I don't, but with these morning ones I do. There, happy?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting with the morning headaches, yesterday and today. Any fever?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm not hot, I checked before we left.
[SEG0048] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's been pale, though. And I'm not making up the snoring. Loud the whole night, then he goes quiet and gasps, like the breathing stops for a second.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not gasp. She watches too much TV. I sleep fine.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): You two aren't going to settle the sleep story in this visit, and this screen has just opened somebody else's results. Any brain tumours in the family, or just the migraines?
[SEG0051] person_4 (CAREGIVER): His mother, migraines, like I said. No tumours I've ever heard of.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. My mother. That's it. The bakkie's on a short bay, by the way, so if we're done...

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nearly. I'm not calling this a tumour. Working impression is a long-standing migraine that's changed, worse on waking, now with vomiting, and I can't fully exclude a pressure problem from this chat alone.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Meaning a scan. I knew it. Medical aid is going to fight me and I haven't got days to sit at the hospital.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not booking one today. If the morning headaches with the vomiting haven't settled in two weeks, then we arrange a CT of the head. If the pain turns sudden and worst-ever, or you get weakness, or you can't keep fluids down, you go to casualty the same day. Don't wait the two weeks for that.
[SEG0056] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And the falling asleep? He was out in the chair at lunch last week, I watched him.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I was resting my eyes. That is not falling asleep. Drop it.

[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): If that daytime sleepiness is still going when I see you again, we can talk about a sleep study, but I'm not ordering it now. Come back in two weeks either way, reception will book it on your way out. Stay on the Panado as you are, no more than four grams of paracetamol in a day, eight of those five hundred milligram tablets at the most, and don't push the sumatriptan up until we know whether it's the fifty or the hundred. I'll finish the note when this thing unfreezes.

spec.situation: Person with long headaches who now has a different pattern (worse in the morning, or with vomiting); takes sumatriptan or paracetamol often; partner says snoring and tiredness too; patient dismisses it. Doctor does a quick neuro exam and orders a scan conditionally.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Current sumatriptan use and 2-3 times weekly supported; frequency detail was reported by caregiver, not patient.
bad.text: sumatriptan (frequency=2 to 3 times a week, indication=headache, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Sumatriptan dose details are incomplete: the repeat/file listed 100 mg PRN, but the patient repeatedly stated he currently takes 50 mg; the 100 mg dose previously caused chest tightness and was changed by the chemist.
Paracetamol/Panado regimen is recorded inaccurately: the patient takes two 500 mg tablets three times a day, sometimes four times a day if the workshop is loud, and said he uses it most days.
Vomiting was initially specifically denied when asked ('No. I don't vomit') and only later revised to morning vomiting with these newer headaches.
Headache location/radiation detail missing: both sides, sometimes more on the left, with a pulse-like pain behind the eye/both eyes.
The patient requested 'something stronger maybe' for the headache.
Negative finding missing: patient denied family history of brain tumours; family history was migraines in mother only.
